candidate.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — immediate nursing intervention for uterine atony/postpartum hemorrhage
candidate.educational_objective: When uterine atony is suspected postpartum, perform fundal massage by stabilizing the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis with one hand while firmly massaging the fundus with the other, and integrate the maneuver into the immediate hemorrhage response.

options.A: Support the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis with one hand while firmly massaging the fundus with the other.
options.B: Use both hands on the fundus and apply forceful downward pressure without stabilizing the lower uterine segment.
options.C: Massage only the lower uterine segment above the symphysis pubis and avoid direct contact with the fundus.
options.D: Delay uterine massage until the uterus remains boggy after all prescribed uterotonic therapy has been completed.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI nursing guidance describes fundal massage by placing one hand on the uterine fundus while the other supports the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis; firm fundal pressure is then used to stimulate contraction. Supporting the lower segment also reduces the risk of uterine inversion during the maneuver. B is incorrect because forceful downward pressure on an unsupported uterus is not the described technique. C is incorrect because the therapeutic massage is directed to the fundus while the lower segment is supported rather than massaged in place of the fundus. D is incorrect because uterine massage is a first-line response when uterine atony is identified and is used as part of the immediate postpartum-hemorrhage response rather than being postponed until uterotonics are exhausted.
candidate.source_claim_supported: For postpartum uterine atony, fundal massage is performed with one hand on the fundus and the other supporting the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis; therapeutic uterine massage is part of the immediate first-response treatment of postpartum hemorrhage rather than a delayed measure.
